description: We are a team of curious innovators passionate about astronomy, space exploration, and technology. Through NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we aim to explore the universe using SPHEREx mission data and develop an interactive platform that makes astronomical observations and changes in the sky easier for everyone to discover and understand.
summary: SPHEREx TimeScope is a web-based tool that helps users explore NASA's SPHEREx infrared observations, view FITS images and metadata, compare observations, and ask questions using a built-in AI assistant.
details:
SPHEREx TimeScope

SPHEREx TimeScope is a web-based application that helps people explore NASA's SPHEREx infrared observations. Users can browse public observation files, view FITS images and their metadata, and compare two observations using visual previews and pixel-difference analysis.

The project also includes a local AI assistant that uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to help users ask questions and understand information about the SPHEREx mission.

The main benefit is making astronomical data easier to access and explore without requiring users to work directly with complex scientific files or specialized software. It is designed for students, educators, and anyone interested in astronomy.

Our goal is to make NASA's open data more approachable and encourage people to explore infrared observations and learn more about the universe. The comparison feature is intended for visual exploration and learning, not to establish scientific discoveries or prove the presence of objects such as Planet X.

The application was developed using Python and Streamlit, with Boto3 for accessing archive files, Astropy for reading FITS data, NumPy and Pandas for data handling, Matplotlib for image visualization, and Ollama with Qwen3:4b and BGE-M3 for the local AI assistant.

The creative aspect of the project is bringing astronomical image browsing, observation comparison, and AI-assisted learning together in one simple interface. During development, we considered usability, access to public NASA data, local computing requirements, and the importance of presenting scientific information responsibly.
